cases.why: The control every other case in this file is measured against.
The load-bearing control. A segment matcher that re-gated the lease would be the compiler taking back an ungating, which is worse than the hole it closes.
The same control after the segment fix, because that fix is exactly what could have widened it.
A prefix match without a whitespace boundary would gate `git pushall`. The boundary is what keeps a prefix rule from becoming a substring rule.
Quoting is respected, so a line that merely NAMES the command is not the command. Without this the gate would block you from describing an attack.
Until 2026-07-28 this matched no gate at all: the matcher prefix-matched the whole command string, so EVERY Gated outward action in this policy was defeated by putting anything in front of it.

Two claims that each held and did not compose: unwrapping was anchored at the start of the command, so a wrapper that was not first was never unwrapped. That is how a gap survives a reader checking either claim alone.
The `$'…'` form, reported by Copilot on #60. The plain-quote spelling turned out to escape the same way, so the fix was wider than the report.

CLOSED at #71, 2026-08-24. Asserted as ESCAPING until that day. A redirection's grammar is closed — an optional fd, one operator, a word — so unlike the leaders below it could be stripped with an edge a reader can check.
The second spelling #71 named.
The third. #71 predicted the fix would flip exactly one assertion; the suite had grown to four, which is why a prediction about a count is checked rather than quoted.
The fourth.
A spelling #71's own table never named. It escaped for a second reason: the segmenter split on the `|`, so the redirection was already in pieces before any strip could see it.
The other unnamed sibling, escaping via the `&` for the same reason. Closing the four named spellings closed these two in the same stroke rather than leaving siblings for someone to come back for.
Redirections stack, so the strip is applied repeatedly rather than once.

The strip's first cut consumed only a non-whitespace word, so this stripped `> "foo` and left `bar" git push --force …` — head `bar"`, no gate, and the segment text corrupted. A fix that closed a hole by a width its own tests never probed. Reported by Copilot round 1; bash was measured running the command after a quoted redirect.

cases.why: The third form a shell word can take. A target reader that handles quotes and not escapes closes two thirds of one hole.
The ordinary spelling of the whole family: redirecting stderr to a path with a space is not exotic.

Copilot round 3, and the THIRD finding of one class: the target reader narrower than a shell word. `"[^"]*"` treated the escaped quote as the closing one, so the span ended early and `bar`/`baz"` became the segment head. Measured escaping, and bash measured creating the file and running the command behind it. Inside a double-quoted span a backslash escapes the next character — the same rule `shellWords` and `commandSegments`'s own quote loop already carried, and the reader did not.

The asymmetry that keeps the fix above from over-reaching. POSIX gives `'…'` no escapes at all, so a backslash there is a literal backslash and the quote after it closes the span. Honouring an escape there would invent a hole rather than close one.

input.command: > foo bar git push --force origin main

cases.why: The false-RED control on the quote-aware target. UNQUOTED, `foo` and `bar` are two words: bash redirects to `foo` and runs `bar`, so `git push --force` is not the command and must not gate. If this ever answers true, the target reader has started swallowing the command behind it.
The control on the strip: a segment that is only a redirection strips to empty and is dropped, rather than becoming a head.

The regression the #71 fix introduced. A `>` a BACKSLASH turned into data is not an operator, and the non-split read one raw neighbour and could not tell — so it un-split a REAL pipe and the force-push after it went invisible. Measured in live bash: `echo \>| tr a-z A-Z` delivers bytes downstream. Caught at HEAD, missed after #71, caught again once the segmenter became escape-aware. Found by the pre-commit checkpoint, which attacked the change rather than reading it.

The sibling of the case above, across `&` rather than `|` — and it is a sibling rather than a duplicate because the two arms of the non-split are separate conditions. Measured in bash: the command after `echo \>&` runs.
The third arm — `<` as well as `>` — added in the same stroke rather than left for whoever meets it, since one carrier fixed and its sibling left is the class this repository names most often.
The control on the repair: making the segmenter escape-aware must not re-gate the Auto spelling on the newly-split path.
Open by decision. Closing the leaders means a named table of command prefixes, and that table has no natural edge — one missing entry buys exactly the false confidence a hole list exists to deny.
`env`, `sudo`, `nice`, `time`, `nohup`, `timeout`, `command`, `stdbuf`, `doas` — the list that has no edge.
The same class.

cases.why: A real shell ignores this; the matcher does not, and asks. A false RED, taken deliberately: deciding where a comment begins gets you a false GREEN when you get it wrong, and a false green costs the laundering the rule exists to prevent.
The case a comment-skipping reader would break. If this ever answers false, the matcher has started treating quoted text as a comment and a gated command has gone invisible.

`matchesRule` promises never to throw, and the promise is load-bearing rather than tidy: gate.mjs catches and steps aside, so an exception silently REMOVES whatever gate was being evaluated. A throw here is a fail-open wearing a stack trace.

The target spelled EXACTLY, with nothing after it. Every other case here carries arguments and so is caught by the whitespace-boundary arm alone; this one is the only case in the corpus that exercises the equality arm. Added because a mutation removing that arm survived all 224 cases.

A LIVE BYPASS until 2026-08-25, and of every Gated shell action rather than this one: one wrapper plus one separator. The composition tested the raw command's segments and each segment's spellings, and never a SPELLING's segments — so `ls && bash -c "…"` was closed while `bash -c "ls; …"` was open. The write matcher never had the gap, because `shellWrites` segments again internally. Found by cli/fuzz-shell.mjs.

input.command: ls && bash -c "x; git push --force origin main"

cases.why: The sibling of the case above, and the reason the repair reads a spelling's segments on BOTH arms rather than one. Fixing only the spelling that was quoted is the class this repository met five times on #336.
The load-bearing control on the 2026-08-25 widening. A repair that re-gated the lease would be the compiler taking back an ungating the maintainer ruled on, which is worse than the hole it closes.

A separator INSIDE a quoted string is data — bash prints it and runs nothing. Added because a mutation disabling quote tracking in `commandSegments` survived the whole corpus: every existing quoted case held a bare command, so none of them would split even if quoting were ignored.
